title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via Server Actions Redirect and Host Header
analysis:
Data flow trace:
1. Source: The untrusted `Host` or `X-Forwarded-Host` request header supplied by an attacker in an HTTP request, alongside a matching `Origin` header.
2. Sanitization/Validation: In `packages/next/src/server/app-render/action-handler.ts`, `handleAction` attempts CSRF protection by checking `originDomain !== host.value`. An attacker directly invoking the Server Action can provide matching `Host` and `Origin` headers (e.g., `Host: attacker.com` and `Origin: http://attacker.com`, or targeting internal network services such as `169.254.169.254` or `internal-service:8080`), bypassing the check.
3. Sink: When the server action executes a relative redirect (via `redirect()`), execution enters `createRedirectRenderResult`. When `process.env.__NEXT_PRIVATE_ORIGIN` is unset (such as in custom server architectures, Edge runtime, or serverless environments), Next.js constructs the origin from `${proto}://${originalHost.value}` and calls `fetch(fetchUrl, { method: 'GET', headers: forwardedHeaders, ... })`. Next.js makes an outbound HTTP request to the untrusted host containing forwarded request cookies and authentication headers, and if the response has content type `text/x-component`, returns the fetched response body directly to the client.

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
```http
POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: 169.254.169.254
Origin: http://169.254.169.254
Next-Action: <action-id-that-performs-redirect>
Content-Type: text/plain

{}
```
Upon execution of the Server Action's redirect (e.g. `redirect('/latest/meta-data/')`), the server makes a `fetch('https://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/')` request, executing an SSRF attack against internal metadata endpoints or internal network services.
